analysis.one_liner: Blocks new trash and hazardous waste incinerators unless strict health, recycling, and community-approval tests are met.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced with 18 Democratic cosponsors in August 1995, it sat in a House subcommittee until the Congress ended, with no Republican support and no committee action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped any new or expanded municipal trash incinerator from getting a permit until 2001, and after that only if the applicant proved the plant would not harm health, would not sit within a mile and a half of schools, churches, hospitals, or drinking water sources, would not fall harder on minority or low-income neighborhoods, and would cost less over its life than recycling and composting. It would have forced incinerator ash into specially designed lined landfills, banned burning batteries, chlorinated plastics, electronics, and yard waste, and imposed similar tests on hazardous waste incinerators, including cement kilns that burn hazardous waste. It never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near proposed incinerator sites — who bear the smoke, ash, and truck traffic — gain the most, along with low-income and minority communities that historically host a disproportionate share of these facilities. The bill also gives local community groups $50,000 technical assistance grants to hire their own experts during permitting, and requires local government approval before any plant is built.

how_it_helps.text: It imposes a five-year moratorium (through 2001) on permits to build or expand municipal solid waste incinerators, and after 2000 allows a permit only if the applicant clears thirteen separate tests, including proof that recycling and composting cannot handle the remaining waste and that full lifetime cost is cheaper than those alternatives.

It bars any new incinerator within 1.5 miles of a school, hospital, church, prison, or drinking water source, and requires applicants to show the facility would not have a disproportionate impact on minority or low-income communities — an early environmental justice safeguard.

It requires incinerator ash to go to dedicated double-lined landfills, bans using the ash for any purpose, and prohibits burning household hazardous waste, batteries, chlorinated plastics, consumer electronics, and yard waste in trash incinerators — the materials that produce dioxin and heavy-metal emissions.

It extends similar health, siting, and community-approval requirements to hazardous waste incinerators — including cement kilns that burn hazardous waste — and requires the applicant to show that the home state and every state shipping waste to the plant runs a toxics use reduction program cutting toxic waste streams by at least 50% within five years.

It gives local community groups a technical assistance grant of at least $50,000 during permitting so they can hire independent experts, and requires the affected local government to approve the project before construction.

analysis.who_pays: Waste incineration companies and cement kilns that burn hazardous waste bear the cost: a multi-year construction freeze, expensive ash-handling retrofits for existing plants, mandated recycling programs, disclosure of their environmental and criminal violation histories, and permit tests stringent enough that few if any new plants could qualify. Municipalities that planned to burn their trash would have had to build recycling and composting systems instead, at least initially at public expense.

drawbacks.text: The requirements were so demanding that they amounted to a near-permanent ban on new incinerators, even where a local government and its residents genuinely wanted one; the bill requires local approval but then layers thirteen federal tests on top, including proof that incineration is cheaper than recycling over the facility's full life.

The diversion mandates were steep — 65% of glass and paper, 80% of metals, 90% of yard waste — and would have forced local governments and haulers to build expensive recycling and composting programs quickly, with costs likely passed to ratepayers.

Blocking incineration can push more waste to landfills, which carry their own contamination and methane risks; the bill requires capacity studies but does not build the recycling infrastructure it presumes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health protections for fenceline communities were real and specific — dioxin from incinerators accumulates in food and water, and the siting buffers and anti-disproportionate-impact tests targeted where the harm lands. But the bill was designed more to stop incinerators than to build the alternative system: it mandated high recycling rates without funding them, and its lifetime-cost test could take years of litigation to satisfy. A narrower version tightening emissions and siting rules might have achieved much of the health benefit at lower cost to municipalities.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 1995 and sent to the House Commerce Committee, which passed it down to two subcommittees; neither acted, and the bill died there when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Richardson (D-NM) introduced the bill on August 4, 1995, joined by Reps. Ed Towns and Maurice Hinchey as original cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Committee on Commerce, which sent it to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment and the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade, and Hazardous Materials on August 17, 1995.
No further action was ever taken: no hearings, markup, or floor vote appear in the record before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.
The bill had 18 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican support in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The waste incineration industry and cement kilns that burn hazardous waste are better off: no construction moratorium, no ash-handling mandates, no disclosure of violation histories, and no toxics-use-reduction requirements were imposed. Municipalities that planned new incinerators also avoided the permit freeze. Communities near existing and proposed plants gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 supporters in the record — the sponsor and 18 cosponsors — were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-run Commerce Committee took no action.

industries.note: A multi-year construction moratorium, a ban on burning batteries, chlorinated plastics, and electronics, strict ash-disposal rules, and thirteen permit tests would have stopped industry expansion and raised compliance costs for existing plants. These facilities profit by burning community waste while nearby residents absorb the dioxin and ash exposure, so the industry's interest in this bill ran against the public's.

industries.industry: Hazardous waste incinerators and cement kilns burning hazardous waste
industries.note: The bill applies its requirements to any facility that burns hazardous waste, including cement kilns, and demands proof that safer disposal technologies do not exist and that states are cutting toxic waste streams 50% in five years. These plants profit from accepting toxic waste whose emissions fall on nearby communities.

Mandated diversion targets — 65% of paper and glass, 80% of metals, 90% of yard waste — would have created guaranteed volume for recyclers and composters. The bill's premise is that these methods are the alternative to burning.

Landfills would receive more waste if incineration were blocked, but states could levy fees on existing incinerators and landfills to fund the required capacity studies, and haulers would bear new recycling program costs. Ash would have to go to costly dedicated double-lined monofills.
